strengths: The paper gives an exact, complete geometric characterization of the (PPV, FOR) feasible region for finite-valued group-calibrated scores, and of the intersection of subgroup regions under sufficiency — filling a real gap, since prior work (e.g., Baumann et al. 2022) relies on continuity/full-support assumptions that fail for discrete scores like COMPAS deciles.

The technical development is clean and largely self-contained: the reduction to a fractional knapsack (Theorem 3.3), the star-convexity argument, the piecewise hyperbolic boundary formula (Eq. 7), and the boundary-tracing algorithm (Algorithm 1) with closed-form quadratic subproblems for loss minimization and separation-deviation minimization are correct and elegant based on the derivations in the appendices (A–H).

Degenerate cases (constant classifiers, empty intersections) are treated carefully in Appendix D rather than ignored, and the distinction between sufficiency as conditional independence vs. predictive parity is handled honestly.
The observation that the boundary of the intersection may contain no deterministic threshold point in either group is a genuinely interesting structural insight with practical implications.
The COMPAS case study is a relevant motivating application and illustrates that group-specific rules are necessary even when the fair optimum is close to the unconstrained one (0.677 vs 0.681).
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is very thin: a single dataset (COMPAS), a single train/test split for estimating the calibration curve and group score distributions, no synthetic experiments, and no comparison against any baseline post-processing method (e.g., Baumann et al. 2022, Canetti et al. 2019, or a generic constrained-LP approach). The claim that deviation-from-separation minimization 'often' achieves performance comparable to the loss optimum is supported by exactly one example.

The framework assumes scores are exactly group-calibrated with known per-group score distributions; in practice these are estimated with error. The paper does not study sensitivity of the solution to calibration/distribution estimation error, which is the main threat to real-world applicability. Using only 20% of COMPAS data to estimate the calibration curve compounds this concern.

The algorithm and analysis are developed for binary A only; the multi-group extension is asserted as 'straightforward' but the pointwise-maximum boundary tracing over more than two subgroup curves, and the separation-deviation analysis (which relies on K = 2P(A=0)P(A=1)|π0−π1|), do not obviously generalize, so the practical scope is narrower than suggested.

The method outputs randomized classifiers, and the paper gives limited discussion of when randomization is unavoidable (or how much randomization the optima require) — a practical and even legal acceptability issue for the motivating high-stakes applications.

Several of the core results (greedy threshold optimality via Dantzig, loss minimized by maximizing p for fixed µ) are conceptually simple; the contribution rests mainly on the careful intersection/boundary machinery. This is respectable but modest, and the significance would be much stronger with broader experimental validation or a multi-group treatment.
No reproducibility artifact (code or data-processing details) is mentioned; exact replication of the COMPAS experiment would require additional specification of the calibration estimation procedure.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: prior post-processing work on sufficiency (Baumann et al., 2022; Canetti et al., 2019) relies on continuity/full-support assumptions that fail for discrete, finite-valued scores, which are common in practice (e.g., COMPAS deciles).

The technical development is clean and largely self-contained: the star-convexity of the feasible region around (π,π), the reduction of the extremal PPV problem to a fractional knapsack (Theorem 3.3), and the explicit piecewise boundary formula (Theorem 3.4) together yield an exact characterization rather than approximations.

The connection between deterministic threshold classifiers and breakpoints of the boundary (µ_k values), and the observation that the fair-optimal boundary may contain no deterministic points (Figure 2), are interesting structural insights.

Appendices A–H provide detailed derivations, including degenerate-case handling (Appendix D) and explicit optimization procedures for both loss minimization and deviation from separation, which supports reproducibility of the method.

The COMPAS case study is a sensible, recognizable testbed, and the finding that the sufficiency-optimal classifier requires group-specific thresholds (S≥7 vs S≥6) concretely illustrates the necessity of group-specific rules.
weaknesses: Empirical evaluation is thin: a single dataset (COMPAS/Broward) with no comparison to any baseline (e.g., Hardt et al. post-processing adapted to sufficiency, Baumann et al., or simple abstention-based approaches). Claims of 'performance comparable to the optimum' for the separation-deviation classifier rest on one example without statistical support (no variance estimates, no repeated splits beyond a single 20/80 split, no other datasets or synthetic experiments varying base rates, calibration error, or support sizes).

The case study ignores estimation uncertainty: empirical calibration curves and score distributions are estimated from finite samples, yet the framework assumes perfectly group-calibrated scores with no sensitivity analysis to calibration error, which is arguably the method's main practical vulnerability.

Scope is narrow: A is assumed binary with the extension to multiple groups called 'straightforward' but not given, and the theory is restricted to post-processing of already group-calibrated scores — a strong assumption in practice, since real scores require recalibration, and the interaction of recalibration error with the exact feasibility geometry is unexplored.

No explicit limitations discussion and no code/artifact or reproducibility statement are provided, despite the method being algorithmic; the algorithmic complexity (e.g., dependence on m0·m1 intervals) is also not formally analyzed.

The application to criminal recidivism (COMPAS, race as protected attribute) receives no ethics discussion: the paper does not address the contested validity of the outcome label, nor the societal implications of recommending group-specific thresholds, which is a notable omission for a fairness paper.

Originality is moderate: the overall structure (post-processing to satisfy a fairness criterion, geometric/ROC-style analysis) closely follows Hardt et al. (2016) and related work; the contribution is an adaptation of this template to the sufficiency/discrete-score setting, with the mathematical novelty concentrated in fairly routine calculus on piecewise-hyperbolic boundaries (Theorems 3.4, Appendices F–H).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically relevant gap: prior post-processing approaches to sufficiency (Baumann et al. 2022) require continuous score distributions with full support, while many deployed systems (e.g., COMPAS decile scores) use finite, discrete scores. The exact characterization for the finite case is a meaningful contribution.

The theoretical development is clean and rigorous. The geometric analysis — star-convexity of the feasible region around (π, π), the connection to the fractional knapsack/greedy thresholding solution (Theorem 3.3), and the piecewise closed-form description of the boundary (Theorems 3.4 and Equation 7) — is worked out completely, with proofs in the appendix covering continuity, endpoint matching, and degenerate cases.

The reduction of sufficiency to membership in the intersection C0 ∩ C1 of subgroup-feasible regions is elegant and leads to a concrete algorithm (Boundary Trace, Algorithm 1) that exactly optimizes a broad class of objectives (any loss, and the deviation-from-separation measure), rather than providing heuristics.

The handling of degenerate cases (constant classifiers within a subgroup, empty intersections, Appendix D) and the explicit treatment of the vertical segment of the boundary show unusual care and completeness; the framework remains well-defined where predictive parity itself is not.

The paper is honest about assumptions and pitfalls: it explicitly notes that re-calibrated COMPAS scores need not be monotone in the original bin ordering, and that results are therefore not directly comparable to prior thresholding analyses; it also carefully separates what is proven from what is observed empirically ('in practice we find...').
weaknesses: The empirical validation is thin. There is a single use case (COMPAS/Broward County) with no baseline comparison — e.g., against the post-processing methods of Canetti et al. (2019) or Baumann et al. (2022) adapted to this setting, or against unconstrained group-wise thresholding. The claim that deviation-from-separation minimization 'often' achieves performance comparable to the loss optimum rests on one dataset and one split, with no uncertainty quantification or repeated runs.

The central assumption of exactly group-calibrated scores is strong, and the paper's pipeline does not account for estimation error: the 20/80 split is used to plug in empirical calibration curves and group score distributions, but there is no finite-sample analysis or robustness discussion of how calibration/estimation error affects the feasibility guarantees and optimality claims of the resulting classifier. This is a significant gap between the exact theory and the applied workflow.

The core mathematical machinery is largely standard — the unconstrained characterization is essentially a greedy-thresholding/ROC-style argument, and the multi-group extension is the pointwise maximum/intersection of the two group regions. The novel technical content, while carefully executed, is incremental relative to known results (Hardt et al., Canetti et al., Chouldechova, Baumann et al., Benger & Ligett).

The framework assumes binary A, with the extension to arbitrary finite supports described only as 'straightforward' but not actually carried out; since multi-group settings are the practically important case for sufficiency (which is fundamentally about conditional independence across all groups), this is a notable restriction.

The optimal classifiers are randomized (mixtures with independent Bernoulli noise, randomized predictions within score bins). The paper does not discuss the practical, legal, or ethical implications of deploying randomized decisions in the high-stakes domains it motivates (bail, lending, admissions), nor whether deterministic approximations exist with bounded degradation.

No code or artifact availability is mentioned, and reproducibility of the COMPAS experiment depends on an unspecified random split; the algorithm is fully specified in the appendices, but the empirical results are not independently verifiable as presented.
There is no explicit limitations or ethics discussion section, which would be appropriate given the sensitive application domain and the assumptions above.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: unlike independence and separation, sufficiency is not preserved by thresholding, and prior work either assumes continuous scores with full support (Baumann et al., 2022) or settles for approximations. The finite, group-calibrated score setting studied here matches practical systems such as FICO and COMPAS.

The technical development is exact and clean. The star-convexity argument, the reduction of the extremal selection rule to a fractional knapsack (Theorem 3.3), the piecewise hyperbolic boundary characterization (Theorem 3.4), and the sweep algorithm over the intersection boundary are all carefully derived, with detailed appendix proofs (A–H) that I spot-checked and found consistent.

The algorithmic payoff is concrete: the loss-minimizing and separation-deviation-minimizing sufficient classifiers reduce to checking endpoints and roots of quadratics on O(m0*m1) intervals, i.e., an efficient and exact post-processing procedure using only calibrated scores and group membership.

The experiments cover three distinct regimes: aggregate statistics (FICO), a directly given discrete score (COMPAS), and a full end-to-end pipeline with estimated group-calibrated scores (ACS Income, 100 train/test splits with bootstrap CIs). The reported parity gaps (4.8e-3 PPV gap vs 3.6e-2 unconstrained) with a small accuracy cost are convincing.

The robustness analysis (Appendix J) provides a linear 2ε bound on predictive parity violations under calibration error, supported by both synthetic and real-data perturbation experiments, which substantially mitigates the exact-calibration assumption.

Limitations are handled honestly: degenerate cases are fully characterized (Appendix D), and the conclusion candidly discusses that exact sufficiency may become infeasible with many groups, framing relaxation as future work rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The framework is restricted to a binary protected attribute; the claimed 'straightforward' extension to arbitrary finite A is nontrivial, since the pointwise maximum of many group boundaries requires a sweep over all pairwise crossings rather than the pairwise quadratic sign test, and the intersection may be empty. This limits applicability to the multi-group settings the paper itself highlights.

The experimental comparison lacks baselines from the prior sufficiency literature (e.g., Baumann et al., 2022 adapted via discretization, Canetti et al., 2019 with abstentions, or OxonFair). The method is only compared to the unconstrained Bayes classifier, so its practical advantage over existing post-processing approaches is not quantified.

Novelty is moderate rather than foundational: the underlying machinery (threshold/soft-threshold classifiers, LP duality, greedy knapsack) is standard, and the main new insight is that sufficiency corresponds to intersecting group-wise feasible regions. The contribution is a careful, exact instantiation rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The claim that minimizing deviation from separation 'often achieves performance comparable to the optimum' rests on three datasets where the ∆sep-minimizer happens to be near-optimal; no theory or broader empirical support for this observation is provided.

FICO and COMPAS experiments are single deterministic case studies without uncertainty quantification (only ACS Income is repeated), and for COMPAS the group-calibration is constructed by the authors themselves (pooled calibration), which is a somewhat artificial setup.
The ∆sep objective is adopted from Benger & Ligett (2025) with limited discussion of why total-variation deviation from separation is the right quantity for practitioners to trade off against loss.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and practically relevant gap: sufficiency (predictive parity) is not preserved by thresholding even when the score is perfectly group-calibrated, and prior post-processing analyses (e.g., Baumann et al., 2022) rely on continuity/full-support assumptions that fail for the discrete scores used in deployed systems.

The technical development is exact rather than heuristic. Theorem 3.3 connects the per-group feasibility problem to a fractional knapsack and gives an explicit soft-thresholding rule; Theorem 3.4 gives a closed-form, piecewise characterization of the boundary of the feasible (PPV, FOR) region, and the intersection boundary of two groups is traced exactly (Algorithm 1) rather than approximated.

The derivation that loss minimization and deviation-from-separation objectives both attain their optima on the boundary of the intersection is a clean reduction, and the appendix computations (quadratic root-finding per interval) make the algorithm concrete and apparently implementable.

The paper is unusually careful about edge cases: degenerate/constant classifiers are handled explicitly (Appendix D), exact feasibility for >2 groups is honestly acknowledged as often failing, and a linear 2ε robustness bound for calibration error (Appendix J) plus empirical checks (Figures 6–7) support the practical use of approximately calibrated scores.

Experiments span aggregate-statistic (FICO), direct-score (COMPAS), and end-to-end (ACS Income) settings, with 100 train/test splits, confidence intervals, and a comparison of the loss-optimal vs. deviation-from-separation solutions.
weaknesses: The core contribution feels incremental relative to existing work. That thresholding calibrated scores violates sufficiency is well known (Chouldechova, 2017; Canetti et al., 2019), and the feasibility-region analysis largely repackages a greedy LP/knapsack solution plus algebraic manipulation into the (PPV, FOR) plane. The main new content is the finite-support treatment, which is a plausible but modest delta over Canetti et al. (2019) and Zeng et al. (2022).

The setting is restrictive in ways that limit significance: A is binary (the multi-group case is deferred to future work, and the authors themselves note the intersection is often empty for more groups), the classifier must be randomized (randomized per-individual treatment at identical scores raises deployment and legal concerns that are not discussed), and exact group-calibration of the score is assumed even though this is unattainable in finite samples in general.

Experimental evaluation lacks baselines. No comparison is made against alternative post-processing approaches that could operate on discretized scores (e.g., the method of Baumann et al. 2022 applied to finite scores, Zeng et al. 2022, or OxonFair, Delaney et al. 2024). The only comparison is against the unconstrained Bayes classifier, so it is impossible to judge whether the exact algorithm meaningfully outperforms simpler or approximate alternatives.

The COMPAS experiment is circular: scores are declared group-calibrated by construction (pooled empirical rates assigned to decile scores, group-specific weights only), so the illustrative 'exact sufficiency' result does not test the method on genuinely calibrated scores; the same critique partially applies to the FICO setup. The ACS experiment is the only end-to-end test and uses a single model/dataset.

The result that minimizing deviation from separation yields accuracy 'often comparable to the optimum' is supported only by three case studies; no systematic analysis of when loss-optimal and ∆sep-minimal solutions coincide or diverge is provided (Figure 2 shows they can differ).

Practical guidance is thin: the paper does not quantify the accuracy cost of sufficiency across settings, does not discuss sample-size requirements for estimating the bin weights P(s|A=a) that the boundary trace depends on, and the robustness bound in Appendix J is worst-case and shown only empirically to be loose.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated gap: prior work on sufficiency (e.g., Baumann et al. 2022) relies on continuity/full-support assumptions, while practical scores are finite-valued. The exact characterization of feasible (PPV, FOR) pairs for finite group-calibrated scores is a clean, complete solution to a practically relevant problem.

The technical development is sound and self-contained. The reduction of the feasibility problem to a fractional knapsack problem (Theorem 3.3), the star-convexity argument, the piecewise hyperbolic boundary characterization (Theorem 3.4), and the algorithmic tracing of the intersection boundary (Algorithm 1) are carefully derived, with proofs and edge cases (degenerate classifiers, empty intersections, boundary construction) treated in detailed appendices.

The paper goes beyond a single objective: the same geometric framework handles both loss minimization under sufficiency and minimization of deviation from separation (via the ∆sep measure of Benger & Ligett 2025), enabling practitioners to compare the two optima explicitly.

Empirical evaluation is reasonable and honest: three case studies (FICO aggregate statistics, COMPAS, ACS Income with an end-to-end pipeline over 100 train/test splits), bootstrap confidence intervals, and a synthetic calibration-error experiment validating the 2ε robustness bound in Appendix J.

Reproducibility is well supported: data sources, preprocessing filters, model training details, and exact (p, q) values attained are all reported, and code is promised. Limitations are discussed candidly (multi-group feasibility becomes restrictive, calibration is only approximate in finite samples), and the calibration-error robustness analysis directly addresses the main practical caveat rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: The setting is fairly restricted: the protected attribute is binary in the analysis (extension claimed 'straightforward' but not shown), and exact sufficiency requires a nonempty intersection of all group-wise feasible regions, which the authors themselves note may fail often as the number of groups grows. This limits immediate applicability.

Experiments are illustrative rather than comparative. There is no empirical comparison against alternative post-processing baselines (e.g., Baumann et al. 2022 under their assumptions, Canetti et al. 2019 with abstention, Zeng et al. 2022, or OxonFair), so the practical advantage of the exact method over approximate relaxations is not directly demonstrated.

Some of the machinery is close to known techniques (fractional knapsack/greedy thresholding, star-convexity arguments); the novelty lies primarily in the exact treatment for discrete scores and the boundary-tracing algorithm, which is a solid but somewhat incremental contribution relative to the existing fairness post-processing literature.

The method relies on randomized decisions, which may be undesirable or legally problematic in high-stakes deployment (e.g., criminal justice, lending); this practical/ethical caveat is not discussed in the impact statement or limitations.

The 2ε calibration-error bound is worst-case and simple; the empirical evidence that violations are much smaller is helpful, but a sharper analysis or distribution-dependent bound would strengthen the practical claims.
